title: Steamboat Springs Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Steamboat Springs wells have a 55 ft median depth, but fractured bedrock can push drilling to 1,100 ft.
h1: Steamboat Springs Colorado Well and Drilling Guide
intro_html:
Well records within 5 miles of Steamboat Springs show a wide range of conditions. The median reported well depth is 55 feet, but the middle half runs from 25 to 350 feet, and the deepest recorded well reaches 1,100 feet. Most permits identify unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers rather than a consistent shallow water-bearing layer.

That spread matters when you are buying land or planning a home. A nearby well can provide useful evidence, but it does not guarantee the same depth or yield on your lot. Review the permit, construction report, pump information, water level, and intended use with the seller and a qualified Colorado driller.

sections.heading: Steamboat Springs well depths vary sharply in mountain bedrock
sections.html:
Depth records around Steamboat Springs are concentrated at the shallow end: 59% of reported wells are under 100 feet. Another 11% fall between 100 and 300 feet, while 24% are 300 to 600 feet and 7% exceed 600 feet. The median is 55 feet, but the 25-to-350-foot middle half is a better warning for budgeting.

Most permits name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, with 1,267 wells in that category. Granite and gneiss do not produce water evenly. Fractures may be shallow, deep, or absent where a driller starts. For a bid, do not rely on the median alone. Have the driller review nearby construction reports and allow for a materially deeper hole if the local pattern supports it.

sections.heading: What Steamboat Springs wells produce
sections.html:
Among the 264 records reporting pump yield, the median is 10.0 gallons per minute. The middle half runs from 5.7 to 15.0 gallons per minute. That is generally a workable production range for household planning, but a pump-yield number is not the same as guaranteed long-term supply or storage in the well.

The records show 2% under 1 gallon per minute, 14% between 1 and 5, 56% between 5 and 15, and 28% above 15. A buyer should pay close attention to the low-yield tail, especially where the proposed home, livestock, irrigation, or other use needs more water. Confirm the test method, recovery, pump setting, storage tank, and legal use before relying on a reported yield.

sections.heading: Water levels near Steamboat Springs and the measured trend
sections.html:
The median static water level is 24 feet below the surface, with the middle half from 8 to 50 feet. These measurements come from only 91 records, so they are useful local clues rather than a complete groundwater monitoring network. Static level also changes with season, recharge, nearby pumping, and how long a well rested before measurement.

By measurement decade, the median was 40 feet below surface in the 2010s and 20 feet in the 2020s. That series does not show a dropping water table; the later reported median is shallower. It also should not be treated as proof that water levels are rising everywhere. Ask for the actual well measurement date and compare it with construction and pumping information.

sections.heading: Permit history and drillers working around Steamboat Springs
sections.html:
The permit record is long-running, with the heaviest activity in the 1990s at 341 permits. The 2000s show 205, the 2010s 162, and the 2020s 133. The newest permit year in the records is 2025. Earlier decades include 134 permits in the 1970s and 134 in the 1980s.

The most frequently recorded drillers are Aztec Drilling Company (Branstetter, Keith) with 210 records, Authorized (Pe, Pg) with 171, and Routt Drilling Co. (Ozbun, Jerald A.) with 70. These are permit-record counts, not a recommendation or a measure of current availability. Before buying, pull the actual DWR construction reports for nearby parcels and confirm who is licensed, insured, and currently taking work.

sections.heading: What a new well can cost in Steamboat Springs
sections.html:
Local ground conditions are fractured mountain bedrock, described in the cost model as granite and gneiss. The typical drilling rate is $65 to $100 per foot. At the 55-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $3,600 to $5,500. That is only the drilling portion, not a ready-to-use water system.

A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at $9,600 to $17,500 at the median depth. A deeper hole can move well beyond that range, while site access, casing, grout, difficult formations, power distance, and water-system design can change the bid. Get a written proposal that separates drilling, casing and grout, pump equipment, trenching, electrical, testing, and permit-related work.

sections.heading: Risks to check before buying or building
sections.html:
Low yield and dry holes are real concerns in fractured bedrock because nearby wells may intersect different fractures. The records contain 2% of reported yields under 1 gallon per minute, and only 264 wells report a pump yield, so the database cannot prove that every parcel has a reliable supply. A DWR permit is not a guarantee of water quantity or quality.

Environmental screening also deserves attention. Within about 10 miles are 17 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 11 historic mine features, and 7 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those mapped locations do not establish contamination at a particular well, but they support testing based on the parcel's setting and well history. Check well construction, casing and grout, septic separation, drainage, and the proposed building location before excavation. Confirm that the intended household, stock, or irrigation use is legally covered; over-appropriated basins may require augmentation planning.

sections.heading: A practical lot check for Steamboat Springs buyers
sections.html:
Start with the exact parcel, then work outward through DWR permits and construction reports. Compare wells in Steamboat Springs with records near Oak Creek, Phippsburg, Clark, Yampa, Hayden, and Walden only as broader context; geology can change quickly across mountain terrain. Give a driller the nearest useful reports before asking for a fixed price.

For an existing home, request the well permit, construction report, pump yield, static level, water-quality results, and recent equipment history. For raw land, budget from the fractured-bedrock cost range rather than the shallow median alone. Confirm access for a rig, power and trench routes, septic siting, and the proposed well's legal use. A Colorado DWR review and a site-specific driller's opinion are more valuable than a countywide average.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Steamboat Springs?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of Steamboat Springs is 55 feet. The middle half runs from 25 to 350 feet, while the deepest record reaches 1,100 feet. Although 59% are under 100 feet, fractured granite and gneiss make individual depth difficult to predict. Nearby construction reports are important when estimating a new well.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Steamboat Springs?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $65 to $100 per foot. At the 55-foot median depth, the drilled hole is about $3,600 to $5,500. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is about $9,600 to $17,500 at that depth. Deeper drilling, access, casing, grout, and site conditions can increase the bid.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Steamboat Springs?
faq.a: Reported yields have a 10.0 gallons-per-minute median, with the middle half from 5.7 to 15.0. About 2% of reported yields are under 1 gallon per minute, while 28% exceed 15. These figures come from 264 records and do not guarantee a new well's performance. Review the test and recovery details before relying on the number.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Steamboat Springs?
faq.a: The permit map does not establish that a particular well is safe to drink. Within about 10 miles are 17 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 11 historic mine features, and 7 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those locations call for parcel-specific testing, along with review of well construction, septic conditions, and the property's history.

faq.q: Can I build a home on a well near Steamboat Springs?
faq.a: A buildable lot needs more than a well permit. Confirm the permitted use, available yield, static water level, septic design, access, power, and building layout. Household use is listed on 52% of permits, while other records cover stock, irrigation, or monitoring. In an over-appropriated basin, an augmentation plan may be needed for the proposed use.
